memory_update.text: Politics theme should be split into at least four industry-chain lanes: defense industrial base, rare-earth/magnet compliance, grid/electrification infrastructure, and trade-compliance/supply-chain visibility software.
Defense bottleneck likely sits below the primes in Tier 2/3 electronics, qualified components, certified manufacturing, testing gates, skilled labor, and sole-source subtier suppliers.
Rare-earth political chokepoint may be non-Chinese-feedstock-qualified magnet supply and customer requalification rather than only mining capacity.

Grid policy bottleneck may include switchgear, electrical distribution equipment, specialty contractors, transmission crews, and utility-qualified suppliers rather than only utilities or renewable developers.
Trade policy creates second-order demand for customs, sanctions, forced-labor, origin-tracing, and supply-chain visibility tools.
Track prime-contractor earnings language for component shortages, Tier 2 constraints, supplier price increases, circuit-board issues, and delivery misses.
Track NDAA, defense appropriations, multiyear procurement, domestic-content rules, waivers, and nonavailability determinations as catalysts for defense and rare-earth nodes.
Track utility capex plans, public grid grants, transmission awards, large load interconnection policy, and data-center power demand for grid equipment and contractor nodes.
Track tariff, sanctions, export-control, and forced-labor enforcement changes for compliance-software and supply-chain visibility nodes.
Need primary-source verification from 10-Ks, 10-Qs, earnings calls, contract notices, DoD award databases, and investor presentations before ranking individual companies in Layer 2B or Layer 3.

Need to distinguish true bottleneck suppliers from companies with generic political exposure by verifying customer concentration, program linkage, backlog, qualification status, capacity constraints, and pricing power.

Need to confirm whether rare-earth compliance rules focus on feedstock origin, magnet location, alloy/powder origin, customer qualification, or waiver pathways because each version redirects value to different nodes.

DCO should be tracked as an underfollowed defense subtier capacity candidate tied to qualified electronic systems, structural systems, prime outsourcing, backlog quality, and long-cycle qualification evidence.
MRCY should be tracked as an underfollowed trusted-defense-electronics candidate tied to radar, EW, C5ISR, missile defense, space, backlog conversion, and funded backlog.

MP should remain a reference anchor for rare-earth magnet compliance, with the key evidence path being NdPr output, magnet ramp, DoD-linked pricing or funding, feedstock qualification, and customer offtakes.
PKE should be tracked as a small-cap qualified aerospace-materials hypothesis tied to composite structures, radomes, possible rocket-motor material exposure, and certification constraints.
POWL should be tracked as an underfollowed grid/electrical-equipment candidate tied to utility-qualified switchgear, power-control systems, backlog, lead times, and data-center or infrastructure mix.

NEO.TO should be tracked as an underfollowed rare-earth processing and magnetic-powder transition candidate, especially if non-Chinese feedstock qualification becomes the binding compliance constraint.

ATRO should be tracked as an underfollowed second-order aerospace electronics and test-systems candidate, but the defense-specific thesis is still weak until government, military-aircraft, and test-system revenue are validated.
GHM should be tracked as a speculative underfollowed naval, space, thermal, vacuum, and turbomachinery systems candidate where qualification and mission-critical equipment exposure may matter.
RBC should remain a reference anchor for qualified bearings and precision components in aerospace and defense, especially where sole-source, military-spec, or long-qualified positions exist.
MYRG should be tracked as an underfollowed grid specialty-contractor candidate linked to transmission backlog, utility capex, labor availability, and public-infrastructure project timing.

Ticker-specific claims for DCO, PKE, ATRO, GHM, POWL, and MYRG require primary-source validation from 10-Ks, 10-Qs, earnings transcripts, contract awards, certifications, and customer/program disclosures before they can move above hypothesis status.

Rare-earth compliance mapping must distinguish mine origin, oxide/feedstock origin, separation, alloying, magnet production, customer qualification, and defense-program approval; MP and NEO.TO should not be treated as equivalent without this chain-level evidence.

Defense subtier bottleneck evidence is strong at the macro level, but each ticker must show actual exposure to constrained programs, qualified capacity, pricing power, sole-source status, customer-funded tooling, or backlog durability.

WIRE should be removed from active public-company candidate lists as an independent ticker; retain only as an acquired Encore Wire asset inside Prysmian for North American electrification/wire capacity mapping.

HPS.A.TO is a high-priority underfollowed grid/electrification candidate because transformer and power-quality exposure maps directly to capacity and qualification bottlenecks; verify backlog mix and margin durability.

LYC.AX should serve as a reference anchor for non-Chinese rare-earth feedstock and separation; later layers must distinguish mine origin, oxide separation, alloying, magnet production, and defense qualification.
GlobalWafers, Siltronic, SUMCO, Wacker, and Entegris map to the semiconductor-materials lane, but the quartz/crucible chokepoint remains indirect and requires supplier-level validation.

LOAR maps to defense subtier components and may fit the underfollowed niche-parts lane, but evidence must separate commercial aerospace aftermarket from defense-specific qualified or sole-source positions.

ATKR needs fresh filing-level validation because policy-linked conduit/raceway demand may be offset by electrical-products price normalization, nonresidential cyclicality, and legal/regulatory issues.

SPSC remains speculative for Politics because current evidence supports supplier-network/EDI functionality but not yet explicit tariff, sanctions, country-of-origin, forced-labor, or customs-compliance monetization.
For all semiconductor wafer names, next layers should verify upstream high-purity quartz/crucible dependency rather than assuming wafer manufacturers capture the chokepoint economics.

QTWO should remain in the speculative_shadow lane until direct filing or call evidence links regulatory-compliance complexity to measurable product demand, revenue, pipeline, or customer budget allocation.
HEI should be treated as a reference benchmark for qualified aerospace, defense, space, and high-reliability component platforms, not as the main underfollowed alpha target in this chunk.

ETN should be used as a reference anchor for grid and power-management demand; subsequent layers should compare it against smaller or purer switchgear, electrical distribution, transformer, and specialty-contractor names.
6501.T should be retained as a grid-equipment and transformer qualification benchmark, but parent-level exposure dilution must be checked before elevating it beyond reference status.

No company filing-level evidence was provided for the current segment mix, backlog, order growth, lead times, pricing power, capacity expansion, or customer concentration of QTWO, HEI, ETN, or 6501.T.
The Politics theme remains better evidenced at the node level than at the ticker level for this chunk; Layer 2C should prioritize primary-source filings and transcripts for each ticker.

summary: Split Layer 2 synthesis. Politics maps less like a single industry and more like a policy-driven demand router. The strongest industry-chain nodes are where government decisions create non-discretionary demand, compliance gates, or capacity scarcity: defense subtier suppliers, rare-earth magnet compliance, grid infrastructure, trade-compliance software, regulated procurement, specialty contractors, and testing/certification. The key Serenity-style angle is to avoid only mapping headline primes, utilities, or mega-cap industrials; the likely bottleneck value may hide in low-attention Tier 2/3 suppliers, qualified materials, certified electronics, non-Chinese feedstock processors, specialty electrical contractors, logistics-compliance tools, and single-source components.

supply_chain_map.node: Defense procurement demand signal
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Government budgets, multiyear procurement, rearmament policy, missile defense, naval programs, space defense, and munitions replenishment determine whether primes and suppliers receive enough demand visibility to invest in capacity.

supply_chain_map.node: Prime defense contractors and platform integrators
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Primes such as major aerospace and defense contractors receive the headline awards, but they depend on hundreds of subtier components and often carry fixed-price margin risk when supply chains tighten.

supply_chain_map.node: Tier 2/3 defense electronics and specialized components
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Specialized circuit boards, ruggedized processing, RF/microwave electronics, mission-critical processors, sensors, and platform-specific electronic assemblies can delay aircraft, missiles, ships, and space systems if qualified suppliers lack capacity.

supply_chain_map.node: Qualified aerospace and defense manufacturing capacity
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Certified suppliers with AS9100, long production history, prime qualification, sole-source positions, or program-specific tooling can become chokepoints because substitution is slow and risky.

supply_chain_map.node: Defense subtier structural systems and aerostructures
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Aircraft, missile, UAV, and space programs require qualified structural assemblies, composite structures, and platform-specific manufacturing capacity that may not scale quickly.

supply_chain_map.node: Precision motion control, actuation, bearings, and engineered components
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Missiles, turrets, aircraft flight controls, helicopters, ships, vehicles, gas turbines, and space systems require precision components with long qualification cycles and potential sole-source positions.

supply_chain_map.node: Rocket motors, propellant-related materials, and qualified composite materials
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Munitions replenishment and missile demand can be constrained by materials, motors, certified composite inputs, and limited production lines rather than by final assembly alone.

supply_chain_map.node: Organic Industrial Base and government-owned surge facilities
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Government-owned depots, arsenals, shipyards, and surge facilities are part of the production bottleneck because years of underinvestment reduced redundancy and skilled labor depth.

supply_chain_map.node: Skilled defense manufacturing labor
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Machinists, welders, electronics technicians, shipyard labor, propulsion specialists, and certified quality staff constrain the ability to turn procurement budgets into physical output.

supply_chain_map.node: Testing, inspection, qualification, and certification gates
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Defense, aerospace, nuclear, submarine, and space systems require long validation cycles; testing capacity and certification history can be as scarce as physical parts.

supply_chain_map.node: Submarine, naval, and subsea mission systems
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: European and U.S. naval rearmament can create bottlenecks in niche submarine hardware, mast systems, pressure housings, subsea communications, naval propulsion, thermal systems, and long-cycle qualified suppliers.

supply_chain_map.node: Rare-earth mining and NdPr production
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Rare-earth inputs are upstream of permanent magnets used in defense, vehicles, drones, motors, guidance systems, and electrification; political restrictions can shift the bottleneck from total capacity to compliant capacity.

supply_chain_map.node: Non-Chinese-feedstock-qualified rare-earth separation and magnet supply
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: If defense rules ban Chinese feedstock rather than only Chinese factory location, the true supply bottleneck is qualified non-Chinese oxide, metal, alloy, powder, and magnet capacity.

supply_chain_map.node: Magnet requalification and customer approval
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Even if nominal magnet capacity exists, defense and aerospace customers must requalify supply chains, which can delay transition and create pricing power for already-qualified suppliers.

supply_chain_map.node: Grid infrastructure and transmission demand
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Politics can drive grid hardening, energy security, electrification, data-center connection policy, reshoring, and public infrastructure capex, all of which pull demand through equipment and construction bottlenecks.

supply_chain_map.node: Switchgear, power-control systems, transformers, and electrical distribution equipment
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Utilities, data centers, industrial sites, and public-grid projects need qualified electrical equipment with long lead times and domestic manufacturing constraints.

supply_chain_map.node: Specialty electrical contractors and transmission construction services
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Even with public funding and equipment orders, grid projects require qualified contractors, crews, permits, utility relationships, and project execution capacity.

supply_chain_map.node: Tariff, sanctions, forced-labor, and customs-compliance software
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Fragmented trade policy increases the cost of cross-border compliance, denied-party screening, customs classification, origin tracing, and supply-chain visibility.

supply_chain_map.node: Supply-chain visibility data and logistics networks
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Companies facing tariffs, sanctions, reshoring rules, and sourcing shifts need software and data tools to track suppliers, shipments, customs exposure, and compliance documentation.

supply_chain_map.node: Domestic-content and Buy America compliance
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Political procurement rules can redirect demand toward domestic or allied suppliers even when cheaper foreign supply exists, creating compliance scarcity in materials, components, and documentation.

supply_chain_map.node: Policy-linked financing, grants, and advance purchase commitments
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Government funding, price floors, offtakes, and guaranteed demand can de-risk capacity expansion for strategic suppliers, especially in defense materials, rare earths, grid infrastructure, and munitions.

supply_chain_map.node: Low-attention public subtier suppliers
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Small and mid-cap suppliers may be misclassified as boring industrials, aerospace components, process equipment, or logistics software even when they sit near policy-created chokepoints.
